stem: In which acute respiratory failure population is NIV preferred over intubation as first-line ventilatory support?
answer: Patients with COPD exacerbation and acute respiratory failure; NIV preferred over invasive mechanical ventilation as initial mode
rationale: NIV avoids complications of intubation (VAP, airway injury) and is associated with improved outcomes in hypercapnic respiratory failure from COPD.

source.book: Society Guideline: Guideline   GOLD 2024 COPD Full Report

stem: What absolute contraindications prevent safe application of NIV?
answer: Facial trauma or burns (impedes mask fitting); fixed upper airway obstruction; active vomiting (aspiration risk)
rationale: These conditions prevent effective mask sealing or create unacceptable aspiration or airway compromise risk.

stem: What complications are specifically associated with NIV that must be monitored?
answer: Gastric insufflation and aspiration, facial skin breakdown, excessively high tidal volumes, patient discomfort (inability to eat or phonate)
rationale: Positive pressure delivered by mask can cause gas swallowing, pressure injury, and volume-related lung injury if not carefully titrated.

stem: What clinical assessment determines when a patient on NIV requires escalation to endotracheal intubation?
answer: Clinical deterioration, ventilatory failure despite NIV, or intolerance to therapy
rationale: Failure to improve oxygenation or ventilation, worsening mental status, or inability to tolerate the mask are indications to proceed to definitive airway.

stem: What was the reported range of invasive mechanical ventilation use in early COVID-19 ICU admissions among COPD patients?
answer: Wide variation: 2.3% to 33% in early reported rates of IMV in hospitalized COPD-COVID patients
rationale: COPD increased risk of ICU admission in some studies but IMV use was heterogeneous across centers.

source.book: Society Guideline: Guideline   GOLD 2024 COPD Full Report

stem: What pathogen is a relatively common cause of both hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia?
answer: Staphylococcus aureus, particularly MRSA (methicillin-resistant S. aureus)
rationale: MRSA colonizes the upper respiratory tract and is a frequent HAP/VAP pathogen requiring vancomycin or linezolid therapy.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Pneumonia  Special Populations & Organisms

stem: What is the reported specificity of MRSA nasal swab testing in the context of S. aureus pneumonia workup?
answer: MRSA nasal swab specificity of 96.1% to 99.2% for MRSA pneumonia
rationale: High specificity supports use of nasal MRSA swab as a de-escalation tool; negative swab argues against MRSA pneumonia.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Pneumonia  Special Populations & Organisms

stem: What interprofessional outcome does coordinated team care improve in staphylococcal pneumonia?
answer: Care coordination among interprofessional team members improves outcomes in staphylococcal pneumonia (HAP/VAP)
rationale: Complex HAP/VAP management requires antibiotic stewardship, respiratory therapy, infectious disease input, and nursing coordination.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Pneumonia  Special Populations & Organisms

stem: What are the pathognomonic findings of dermatomyositis on physical examination?
answer: V-neck sign, shawl rash, heliotrope rash; proximal muscle weakness (deltoids, hip flexors, neck flexors); mild muscle tenderness; distal strength preserved; DTRs normal
rationale: DM has characteristic cutaneous findings plus proximal myopathy; distal sparing and preserved reflexes help distinguish from neuropathy.

stem: What autoantibody in dermatomyositis is associated with acute onset disease, V-neck sign, and shawl rash?
answer: Anti-Mi2 (directed against helicase); associated with acute disease onset and classic cutaneous findings
rationale: Anti-Mi2 targets nuclear helicase; this MSA predicts florid cutaneous DM with acute onset.

stem: Which patient factors predict occult malignancy in inflammatory myopathy?
answer: Male gender, older age at onset, presence of dysphagia, absence of interstitial lung disease
rationale: DM is a paraneoplastic syndrome in a subset; these features identify patients warranting malignancy screening.

stem: What is the pathophysiology of vascular injury in dermatomyositis?
answer: Complement factor C3 activation -> C3b/C4b deposition -> C3bNEO neoantigen -> C5b-C9 membrane attack complex deposits on muscle capillary endothelium -> vasculopathy
rationale: DM is a complement-mediated vasculopathy; capillary loss causes perifascicular muscle ischemia rather than direct T-cell myocyte attack (unlike polymyositis).

stem: What feature distinguishes inclusion body myositis from dermatomyositis on muscle biopsy and treatment response?
answer: IBM shows characteristic inclusion bodies on biopsy and is refractory to corticosteroids (unlike DM/PM which respond)
rationale: IBM is a degenerative myopathy with distinct pathology; immunosuppression does not alter its course.

stem: What are the most common drug causes of drug-induced myopathy that must be excluded before diagnosing DM/PM?
answer: Statins, alcohol, penicillamine, colchicine, glucocorticoids, zidovudine, and antimalarials
rationale: Drug-induced myopathy is reversible on withdrawal; these agents must be excluded before attributing weakness to idiopathic inflammatory myopathy.

enabling_conditions: Adults 40-60; DM also in children; female predominance; environmental triggers (UV, myositis-associated viruses)
pathophysiology: DM: complement-mediated capillary vasculopathy -> perifascicular ischemia; PM: CD8+ T-cell direct myocyte invasion
time_course: Subacute weeks to months; acute onset in anti-Mi2 DM
key_features: DM: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, V-neck/shawl sign, proximal weakness, elevated CK/aldolase, myositis-specific antibodies; PM: no skin findings
consequence_if_missed: ILD (anti-synthetase syndrome), cardiac involvement, occult malignancy, aspiration from pharyngeal weakness

discriminator: DM: skin rash, complement vasculopathy, responds to steroids, paraneoplastic association; IBM: no rash, inclusion bodies on biopsy, distal + asymmetric weakness, steroid-refractory

stem: What temperature range does ACLS recommend for TTM in patients who do not follow commands after ROSC?
answer: 32-36 degrees C; use controlled cooling devices; active cooling is supported by current guidelines
rationale: TTM reduces ischemia-reperfusion brain injury after cardiac arrest by decreasing cerebral metabolic demand.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   ACLS  Non Shockable Rhythms (PEA & Asystole)

stem: What are the four main components of comprehensive post-cardiac arrest care?
answer: Hemodynamic support, mechanical ventilation, targeted temperature management, and identification/treatment of reversible SCA causes
rationale: Ischemia-reperfusion injury from cardiac arrest affects multiple organ systems requiring simultaneous multi-system interventions.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   ACLS  Non Shockable Rhythms (PEA & Asystole)

stem: What is the initial evaluation after ROSC to identify reversible causes of cardiac arrest?
answer: Evaluate for possible SCA causes; initial assessment includes clinical evaluation for reversible etiologies (Hs and Ts)
rationale: Treating the underlying cause prevents recurrent arrest; coronary angiography for suspected ACS, CT for structural causes.

stem: How does survival rate change with each minute of delayed defibrillation in ventricular fibrillation?
answer: Survival decreases approximately 10% per minute without defibrillation in VF; defibrillation within 3-5 minutes is ideal
rationale: VF causes progressive global ischemia; early defibrillation restores perfusion before irreversible myocardial and cerebral injury occurs.

stem: What ACLS monitoring parameters should be continuously assessed during CPR to improve performance?
answer: Chest compression rate and depth, chest recoil, ventilation rate and force; accelerometer-equipped devices provide real-time feedback
rationale: Real-time feedback corrects suboptimal CPR performance and improves ROSC rates.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   ACLS  Non Shockable Rhythms (PEA & Asystole)

stem: What medications decrease progression of ankylosing spondylitis and related spondyloarthropathies including psoriatic arthritis?
answer: Anti-TNF-alpha agents (infliximab, etanercept, adalimumab, golimumab) decrease progression when administered early
rationale: TNF-alpha drives inflammation and structural joint damage in spondyloarthropathies; early biologic therapy halts radiographic progression.

stem: What infectious and malignant risks accompany anti-TNF therapy in spondyloarthropathies including psoriatic arthritis?
answer: Increased risk of serious infection and development of lymphoma with anti-TNF agents
rationale: TNF is required for granuloma maintenance and immune surveillance; blockade impairs defense against intracellular pathogens and may promote lymphoma.

stem: Which cardiovascular structure is affected by psoriatic arthritis and related spondyloarthropathies via aortic annulus dilation?
answer: Aortic valve (aortic regurgitation) from dilation of the aortic annulus
rationale: Inflammation causes annuloaortic ectasia, disrupting coaptation of aortic valve leaflets and causing regurgitation.

stem: Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, which part of the spine is typically spared in RA but involved in psoriatic/reactive arthritis?
answer: RA typically spares the spine except cervical zygapophyseal joints; psoriatic and reactive arthritis can involve the full spine with axial disease
rationale: Spondyloarthropathies have characteristic sacroiliac joint and axial involvement; RA is a predominantly peripheral arthritis.

stem: What extraspinal features distinguish psoriatic arthritis and reactive arthritis from RA?
answer: Extraspinal manifestations (skin psoriasis, eye inflammation, GU/GI features) are usually more prominent than spinal disease in psoriatic and reactive arthritis
rationale: Spondyloarthropathies are multisystem diseases with characteristic extra-articular manifestations reflecting shared HLA-B27-associated inflammation.

stem: What are the upper limits of normal QTc, and how is the QT interval measured?
answer: Normal QTc <=460 ms; borderline: 460-479 ms (female), 450-459 ms (male); measure from QRS onset to end of T wave in lead with T wave >2 mm (best in II, V5)
rationale: QTc correlates with ventricular repolarization time; prolongation increases risk of re-entrant arrhythmia (torsades de pointes).

stem: What is the risk relationship between QTc prolongation and torsades de pointes?
answer: QTc prolongation is a risk factor for torsades de pointes; this risk increases substantially with depressed LVEF
rationale: Prolonged repolarization creates a vulnerable window for early afterdepolarizations that trigger the characteristic polymorphic VT of TdP.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Hypocalcemia  Causes and Management

stem: When does ibutilide-associated torsades de pointes typically occur, and who is at highest risk?
answer: Most cases occur within 30 minutes of the last dose; rarely reported up to 2 hours later; risk increased with depressed LVEF
rationale: Ibutilide's class III antiarrhythmic effect prolongs repolarization; systolic dysfunction amplifies TdP risk.

source.book: Society Guideline: Guideline   ACC AHA 2023 Atrial Fibrillation

stem: What electrolyte disturbance must be corrected to reduce TdP risk, and what is the pathophysiology?
answer: Hypokalemia: maintain K+ >=4 mEq/L; hypokalemia potentiates early afterdepolarizations by reducing outward K+ repolarizing current, further prolonging QT
rationale: K+ current (IKr) is essential for phase 3 repolarization; hypokalemia blocks IKr and amplifies QT prolongation from any cause.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Hypocalcemia  Causes and Management

stem: What is the concern with dronedarone in patients with advanced heart failure and AF?
answer: Dronedarone had higher mortality in NYHA class III-IV HF patients with AF compared to placebo; not recommended in severe HF
rationale: Dronedarone's negative inotropic and proarrhythmic effects are poorly tolerated in severely depressed cardiac function.

source.book: Society Guideline: Guideline   ACC AHA 2023 Atrial Fibrillation
